This right is jurisprudentially grounded on the sovereign equality of states and national self-determination. Second, the theoretical connotation of NDR. We interpret its theoretical connotation from three perspectives. First, theoretically, it represents a shift from regarding development as a primary human right to recognizing the state-centered dimension of the right to development. NDR does not negate the primacy of the individual right to development. Instead, it highlights that the realization of the right to development at a state level presupposes state sovereignty and a fair international order. It expands subjects and dimensions for the right to development within the traditional human rights system. It situates the proposition that development is a primary human right precisely within the international law framework. Rather than putting NDR against individual rights to development, it regards the former as a structural guarantee for the realization of the latter. The state as a core subject to the state as a dual status subject.

States assume dual subject status in the system of right to development.

On the other hand, states are obligation bearers.

They shall formulate domestic development policies, safeguard individual rights to development, and fulfill obligations for international development cooperation. NDR is not groundless. Its core elements are deeply embedded in existing sources of international law and key UN documents. At present, it mainly functions as a soft law principle and opinio juris, providing important evidence for the formation of customary international law. For instance, Article 1, 55, and 56 of the Charter of the United Nations set the purpose of promoting international cooperation in solving international problems of an economic, social, cultural, or humanitarian character. This furnishes the fundamental treaty law basis for calls for international cooperation and a just international economic order. The UN Declaration on the Right to Development, Article 1, clarifies that the holders of the right to development include every human person and all peoples. Article 2, paragraph 3 of the same declaration establishes the dual legal status of states, both as holders and bearers of the obligations for the right to development. Article 3, paragraph 1 and 4 offer direct normative grounds for states to invoke international cooperation obligations. The Vienna Declaration and Program of Action reaffirms that the right to development is universal and inalienable and forms part of a fundamental human right, firmly embedding NDR within the international human rights law system. The principle of permanent sovereignty over natural resources safeguards states' autonomy over domestic development resources.
